title: The Gateless as the Dharma Gate
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Only realize the direct perception of one’s own mind, and deluded thoughts will not arise; there will be peace and joy, and worldly affairs will cease forever.

inline.s: Only realize the direct perception of one’s own mind, and deluded thoughts will not arise; there will be peace and joy, and worldly affairs will cease forever.
Question: Mazu said the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra (the Laṅkāvatāra Jewel Sutra) states:
“The words of the Buddha take the mind as their essence, and the gateless is the Dharma gate.”
What does this mean?

Answer: “The words of the Buddha take the mind as their essence” means that the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra takes the mind as its essential principle. The entire Laṅkāvatāra Jewel Sutra consists of only a single chapter, whose title is: “The Mind of All the Buddhas’ Words.” “The mind of all the Buddhas’ words”: all the words of the Buddhas teach only this mind. In other words, all Buddhas expound this mind. Because

one’s own mind is the Buddha; all realms are produced only by karma and manifested only by the mind; whether there is birth-and-death or nirvāṇa lies entirely in the turning of this one mind, and there is no other dharma.
The mind is so important that all the Buddhas expound the mind. Master Hanshan says:
“Because
(since)
this sutra directly points out that the store of consciousness of sentient beings is none other than the Tathagata-garbha, and reveals the realm present in everyday life,
enabling one to observe in accordance the direct perception of one’s own mind and suddenly realize the self-awakened holy wisdom of the Buddhas
; therefore it is called ‘the mind of the Buddha’s words.’”
(Notes from the Pavilion for Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra Jewel Sutra)
[The entire text is only one chapter] According to Master Hanshan’s Notes on Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra:
“This sutra has forty fascicles. This
(the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra transmitted to China)
is only a tenth of it.”
[The mind of all the Buddhas’ words] The Tang translation (the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sutra) says:
“The mind taught by all Buddhas.”

[The direct perception of one’s own mind] “Direct perception” (pratyakṣa) is the ability to intuit the existence of something directly, without the deliberation of consciousness — that is, immediate knowledge. (Knowledge gained by inference is “inferential knowledge,” anumāna.) To realize the direct perception of one’s own mind is to know, like a mirror reflecting objects, the realm manifested by one’s own mind, without discursive thought or calculation. This sutra says:
“Only realize the direct perception of one’s own mind, and deluded thoughts will not arise; there will be peace
(wěn, “stable”)
and joy, and worldly affairs will cease forever.”
The Zongjing Lu (Record of the Mirror of the School) says:

“The Buddha said: ‘Only realize the direct perception of one’s own mind, and deluded thoughts will not arise; there will be peace and joy, and worldly affairs will cease forever.’ ‘Peace and joy’ is quiescence, wonder, and constancy; ‘worldly affairs cease forever’ means that clinging has been cut off. One may say that to meet the perfect and complete treasure-house is to suddenly end all seeking and hoping, to arrive at the nirvāṇa of eternal bliss with nowhere further to go; it is the juncture of the ordinary and the holy, like reaching one’s homeland; it is the basis of delusion and awakening, having exhausted the very root. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: ‘The vajra treasure-house lacks nothing and diminishes nothing.’”
Master Hanshan’s Notes on Contemplating the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says:
“By the direct perception of one’s own mind, neither holy nor ordinary is established, and everything is negated, thereby revealing the meaning of ultimate awakening within arising and ceasing.”
Patriarch Bodhidharma’s Gate of Pacifying the Mind says:

“Whoever still has a mind that discriminates and calculates the direct perception of one’s own mind is entirely in a dream; if one knows the mind in its quiescent extinction, where there is no place for any thought, this is called right awakening.”
Master Hanshan also says:
“As for the chapter on the mind of the Buddha’s words,
this sutra directly points to the one quiescent mind as its essence, and takes realization through the self-awakened holy wisdom as its aim
(Supplement to the Laṅkāvatāra)
“The words of the Buddha take the mind as their essence, and the gateless is the Dharma gate”:
The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp records:
(Mazu)

one day said to the assembly: Each of you must believe that your own mind is the Buddha, and that this very mind is the Buddha-mind. The great master Bodhidharma came from southern India and traveled personally to China, transmitting the supreme-vehicle Dharma of the one mind so that you might awaken. He also cited the text of the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra to seal the mind-ground of sentient beings, fearing that you, being inverted, would not believe in this Dharma of the mind, which each of you possesses. Therefore the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says:
“The words of the Buddha take the mind as their essence, and the ‘gateless’ is the Dharma gate.”

It also says: One who seeks the Dharma should have nothing to seek; apart from the mind there is no other Buddha, and apart from the Buddha there is no other mind. Do not grasp the good nor reject the evil; rely on neither of the two extremes of purity and defilement
(hù)

; realize the emptiness of the nature of offenses — thought after thought is unobtainable, because there is no self-nature. Therefore the three realms are mind only, and the myriad phenomena are all stamped by the one seal
[The myriad phenomena are all stamped by the one seal]

The myriad phenomena are all stamped with the one Dharma-seal. [The one Dharma-seal] Also called the one seal of the true mark and the seal of the true mark of all dharmas. A Dharma-seal is the seal and tally of the Buddha-Dharma; it is the seal of truth handed down from Buddha to Buddha, and it is the standard of the Buddha-Dharma — whatever does not accord with the Dharma-seal is not the Buddha-Dharma. The Mahāyāna teaching takes the true mark of all dharmas as its root, and whatever departs from it belongs to the words of demons. [The true mark of all dharmas] The “true mark” is the actual state of affairs; “the true mark of all dharmas” is the actual state of affairs of all dharmas. The Buddha-Treasury Sutra says:
“What is called the true mark of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty and without anything whatsoever.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says:
“All dharmas are like illusory appearances, and the Tathagata, abiding within them by the power of skillful means, is without any defilement or attachment.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“The bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, in accordance with the true mark, without inversion, without wavering, without retreat, without turning.”
(see
The True Mark of All Dharmas

[Holy wisdom] The Tathagata’s wisdom of the essential nature of the Dharma-realm, namely the wisdom that realizes “all dharmas are originally unborn,” also called the pure wisdom of the Dharma-realm. This sutra says:

“Mahāmati! The ultimate mark of the self-awakened holy wisdom is this: one is without any calculation or attachment to any mark of dharmas, attains the body of the illusion-like samādhi, and advances in practice toward the stage of the Buddhas.”
It also says:

“The Buddha told Mahāmati: What the former sages knew they handed down from one to another — that deluded thoughts are without self-nature. The bodhisattva-mahāsattva, alone in a quiet place, observes with his own awakening, not depending on another, free of views and deluded thoughts, advancing higher and higher, until he enters the stage of the Tathagata — this is called the mark of the self-awakened holy wisdom.”

The gateless is the Dharma gate.” “Gateless” does not mean there is no gate. Here “no” (wu) is not the “no” of “having and not having,” but the true mark of all dharmas that transcends both — originally there is not a single thing; and here “gate” means a path, a key. “The gateless is the Dharma gate” means:
to take “no” as the gateway of practice.

In other words: by the principle of the true mark of all dharmas, pierce through the dream of ignorance and perfectly accomplish the Buddha-way. And what does one use to pierce through? One uses the mind. Hence it is said: “The words of the Buddha take the mind as their essence.” In the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra, this method of practice — “no” — appears everywhere; to sum it up:

the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty, the eight consciousnesses and the two selves are both dismissed, the two dharmas of being and non-being are entirely left behind — and one realizes the self-awakened holy wisdom and enters the stage of the Tathagata.
— This is the main content of the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra (see
Selected Annotations on the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra
